claims.text: Redis and MySQL are separate consistency domains; Redis MULTI/EXEC does not create a shared atomic transaction with MySQL, so the default design treats the database as authoritative and Redis as rebuildable cache state with an explicit consistency target.

The normal write path commits the authoritative database first and invalidates Redis afterward; failure after commit is repaired by retry/TTL/CDC/reconciliation, while a concurrent old read can still refill stale data after deletion and therefore needs an explicit race-window mitigation.

Delayed double-delete is a best-effort way to remove a stale value reinserted by a concurrent old read; a fixed delay cannot prove strong consistency and the second invalidation still needs retry/TTL/repair coverage.

MySQL binlog plus Canal/CDC can asynchronously derive cache invalidation or refresh from committed database changes, but the consumer still needs checkpointing, replay, retry, idempotency, lag monitoring and log-retention recovery; this is eventual repair rather than synchronous strong consistency.

If CDC refreshes values rather than only deleting keys, stale or duplicate events must not regress a newer cache version or resurrect deleted state; comparable versions/change positions plus periodic database-to-cache reconciliation provide a concrete non-regression and recovery boundary.

Capacity and SLO numbers are explicitly labeled as illustrative assumptions, while the production design calls for hit/miss load, DB headroom, invalidation latency/failure rate, CDC lag/oldest-event age, reconciliation throughput, fault injection, rollout and rollback observability instead of fabricated project metrics.

findings: The frozen repository source contains both Redis/database and Redis/MySQL consistency variants and explicitly preserves delayed double-delete and Canal/binlog as interview entities; the candidate covers both variants rather than narrowing to one trick.

The frozen primary-source packet establishes the database-as-authoritative cache-aside boundary, Redis-local transaction limits, TTL expiration semantics, MySQL binlog availability/retention, Canal incremental consumption, and the repository's executable non-regression repair experiment.

The candidate turns those facts into a complete scenario design: DB-first invalidation, the old-read refill race, delayed double-delete as best-effort mitigation, retry/outbox or CDC repair, checkpoint/idempotency/version boundaries, reconciliation, observability, fault injection, and a stricter read-after-write path when eventual consistency is insufficient.

The candidate labels capacity and SLO numbers as illustrative assumptions, does not claim cache-aside/double-delete/Canal provide strong consistency, and does not fabricate production topology, incidents, metrics or personal project experience.
